metadata.title: The Reversal Curse
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 2 — why an LLM that knows A→B cannot answer B→A: the Autoregressive Probability Rule, the one-way weights it builds, and the bidirectional control experiment that proves the flaw is architectural.

beats.narration_text: I am Onkar Bhujbal, a software engineer. If an AI knows Tom Cruise's mother is Mary Lee South, why doesn't it know Mary Lee South's son is Tom Cruise? Because large language models do not learn facts. They learn probabilities. This is a logic flaw called the Reversal Curse.

the last output line names the flaw: THE REVERSAL CURSE

output: Q: Who is Tom Cruise's mother?   →   Mary Lee South.
Q: Who is Mary Lee South's son?  →   I don't know.
Same fact. One direction. THE REVERSAL CURSE.

beats.honesty_note: The Tom Cruise / Mary Lee South pair is the canonical published example of this failure and is used by the source script. The exchange shown is the script's own, not a transcript of a live model run — no specific model or version is named, so nothing here dates or misattributes.

beats.narration_text: A language model doesn't store facts it can look up from either end. It stores which word tends to follow which. That is why A leads to B, but B never leads back to A.

beats.authoring_note: Single-word trigger: BrutalistHesitantWriter matches whitespace-delimited word cores only, so phrase-level correction cannot match. 'facts'->'directions' is the reel's actual misconception and corrects the sentence. Keep the typed text near 75 chars so it finishes inside the audio window.

beats.narration_text: To understand this, we use the Autoregressive Probability Rule. One: models are trained to predict the next word, strictly left to right. Two: every word's probability is conditionally dependent only on what precedes it. Three: training updates neural weights in one direction. A leads to B does not map the path from B back to A.

beats.narration_text: So let's draw what those billions of training pages actually build inside the model — not the facts we imagine are stored in there, but the directed graph the weights really encode.

beats.narration_text: Apply the framework to the training data. The model ingests billions of pages where Tom Cruise is the subject and Mary Lee South is the object. It strengthens the unidirectional weights from left to right. When you prompt with the mother's name first, the conditional probability chain is completely empty. The neural path literally does not exist in reverse.

beats.narration_text: So how do we prove this is an architectural flaw and not just bad data? We test a bidirectional model, like BERT. BERT doesn't read left to right. It masks words in the middle of sentences and reads from both ends at once. Bidirectional models pass the reversal test easily — which puts the flaw squarely in autoregressive, left-to-right training.

beats.narration_text: Test this on your own local models. Find a lesser-known indie film. Ask the AI who directed it — it will likely know. Then open a fresh chat and ask it to name a film by that specific director. Watch it fail.

props.title: reversal_test.txt
props.code:
PROMPT 1:  Who directed [obscure indie film]?
           → it will probably answer correctly

# open a FRESH chat — no history, or you have
# handed it the answer in the context window

PROMPT 2:  Name a film directed by [that director].
           → watch it fail

# TASK: test a local LLM with asymmetrical facts.
# The rarer the fact, the cleaner the result.

beats.authoring_note: The 'fresh chat' caveat is added, not in the source script: asking both questions in one session puts the answer in the context window and the test silently passes for the wrong reason. Without it the scaffolded task does not actually falsify anything.

beats.narration_text: And when it fails, here is the prompt worth running next. Ask a model to list every fact it knows about one obscure person, then ask which of those facts it could recover if you started from the other end. Make it mark each one. What you get back is a map of its own blind spots — written by the model that has them.
